newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Court ruling fuels calls for Australian tax reform.
newsitem.headline: Court ruling fuels calls for Australian tax reform.

text.p: A landmark ruling by Australia's highest court striking down some state taxes on Tuesday fuelled calls for a full-scale overhaul of the complex and outdated tax system.
Business groups urged the national government to seize the opportunity to rewrite the tax system, and state and territory governments urged reforms to federal-state financial relations.
"Fundamental tax reform must be an inevitable consequence of the High Court's decision," Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry chief executive Mark Paterson said in a statment.
"The decision confirms the need to urgently address deficiences in federal-state financial relations as part of fundamental reform of the tax system."

In a four to three majority, the full bench of the High Court earlier on Tuesday ruled that state business franchise fees levied on retailers of tobacco, alcohol and petrol were in fact excise duties, which only the national government can raise under Australia's constitution.
The decision means the national government will have to pass legislation to collect the money on behalf of the states and return it to them.

A leading tourism industry group, Tourism Council Australia, said the decision highlighted the need for tax reform and was also a warning to states not to hike taxes and other charges as an easy way to cover budget deficits.
"Industries like tourism, which are affected by taxes at both a state and federal level, are crying out for a taxation overhaul," said council chief Bruce Baird.
"What is needed is a complete review of the Australian taxation system.
"Today's decision sends a warning signal to state governments not to levy taxes at random in a bid to fill budget shortfalls -- as such measures will come under increasing scrutiny."
Part of the court's reasoning for overturning the state excises was the fact that they had dramatically increased over levels previously approved by the court.
The states and territories already rely on Canberra for half their income, divided up at a traditionally acrimonious annual meeting of state, territory and national leaders.

The Taxation Institute of Australia said the ruling meant a consumption tax on goods and services -- an option leading the debate on tax reform -- was inevitable as the national government and states faced a shrinking indirect tax base.

Australia's Liberal-National government, stressing the need for tax reform, has called for a national debate on the issue, but ruled out a consumption tax in its first term, due to expire by mid-1999.
The national, state and territory governments are now negotiating how Canberra can replace the state levies and how to share the money among the states and territories.
National Treasurer Peter Costello said federal help was conditional on prices remaining steady -- flagging the possibility of a rebate in some states.

The ruling is likely to see prices for petrol, alcohol and tobacco rise at first in some states, because the national government cannot levy different rates in different areas and is expected to set its rates at the highest existing levels.
Currently, the franchise fees vary between states and one, Queensland, has no charge at all on petrol.
